Twenty minutes to take $6.3 billion, and by the weekend Binance was reopening bitcoin and ether withdrawals after, in Reuters' phrase, covering the bulk of what was stolen. The headline detail is North Korea. The one I can't stop looking at is the "covering."

I only have the headlines, so I don't know where the money came from. But think about what just happened structurally. A private company with no deposit insurance and no central bank behind it lost something close to the size of a mid-sized regional bank failure, and made customers whole in roughly the time it takes the FDIC to schedule a press call. Every critique of crypto I've read for years says this is the scenario where it all comes apart. The exchange has to be its own lender of last resort, and the lender is the borrower. And yet here is the line of customers, getting paid.

I'm not going to call that robust. One data point where the tail event arrived and the thing didn't snap is also exactly what a fragile system looks like right before the version that does snap. Binance may simply have had a fat enough balance sheet this once, and a fat balance sheet is a fact about the past.

What amuses me is the company it's keeping this week. A site yesterday ran the headline that US stocks now swing like meme tokens, while Treasuries rally as the safe harbor from AI worries. Meanwhile the exchange everyone assumed was the weak link posted the more orderly recovery of the two.

Which asset class is the bank, I wonder, and which is the run?
